account: On 23 June 2022 researchers at University Hospital Basel with no tie to Withings published a study of 317 patients. They found that the ScanWatch measured the corrected QT interval (QTc) automatically in 56% of them. They also found that 29% of its measurements differed from manual readings by more than 30 ms. They wrote that its algorithm needed improvement for clinical use. A case report published on 4 July 2024 describes an asymptomatic 39-year-old man who came to the cardiology outpatient clinic of University Medical Centre Mannheim, Germany, because of QT prolongation recorded with his Withings ScanWatch. The report gives no event dates. He had made the watch's single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings out of curiosity. The watch displayed values such as QT 506 ms and QTc 457 ms. The resting 12-lead ECG at his first visit gave a QTc of 522 ms. Genetic screening found a previously unpublished nonsense variant in KCNH2, which established congenital long QT syndrome. Nadolol 40 mg daily shortened his QTc by 50–70 ms to 430 ms. His 7-year-old daughter carried the same variant with a borderline QTc of 460 ms and was also prescribed nadolol. The case report states that the father is followed at regular intervals without further interventions.

ai_role.statement: The watch's automated ECG analysis displayed the QT and QTc values that prompted the clinic visit. No automatic alert is described. The report does not say who first noticed the values. Diagnosis rested on clinical ECGs and genetic testing.
